name: Buddhaghosa

tradition.text: came to Lanka in the reign of King Mahānāma (Cūḷavaṃsa)

places: Magadha (near the Bodhi tree, per Cūḷavaṃsa)

realization_account.text: The Cūḷavaṃsa tells that he was a brahmin versed in the Vedas, converted by the elder Revata, and that the gods twice hid his Visuddhimagga so that he wrote it three times, each copy identical — proof that he was fit to render the commentaries; the Burmese Buddhaghosuppatti adds further legends.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: The great 5th-century commentator of the Mahāvihāra, author of the Visuddhimagga and of the Pali commentaries on the Vinaya, the four Nikāyas and the Abhidhamma, which fixed Theravāda orthodoxy.

name: Revata (teacher of Buddhaghosa)
summary: The elder in India who, according to the Cūḷavaṃsa, converted the brahmin Buddhaghosa and sent him to Lanka to render the Sinhala commentaries into Pali.
notes: Disambiguated from Revata of the Second Council.

name: Buddhadatta
summary: Commentator and manual author from Uragapura (Uraiyūr) in the Cola country, said to have been a contemporary of Buddhaghosa; author of the Abhidhammāvatāra and the Vinayavinicchaya.

name: Dhammapāla

scholarly.text: 6th c. CE (contested; some place him later)

summary: Commentator of Badaratittha (near Kāñcīpuram in South India) who wrote the Paramatthadīpanī on seven Khuddaka books, the Visuddhimagga sub-commentary Paramatthamañjūsā and sub-commentaries on the Nikāya commentaries.
notes: Whether the Khuddaka commentator and the ṭīkā author are one person is debated by scholars.

name: Culla-Dhammapāla
summary: A later Dhammapāla to whom some attribute the Abhidhamma Anuṭīkā and the Saccasaṅkhepa.

name: Ānanda (author of the Mūlaṭīkā)
summary: The elder credited with the root sub-commentary on the Abhidhamma commentaries.

name: Upatissa (author of the Vimuttimagga)
summary: The elder named as author of the Vimuttimagga, a manual of the path earlier than the Visuddhimagga; nothing else is known of him with certainty.
notes: Dhammapāla's sub-commentary identifies some anonymous views cited in the Visuddhimagga as Upatissa's (as remembered; not checked).

name: Saṅghapāla (Sengqiepoluo 僧伽婆羅)
summary: Monk from Funan who translated the Vimuttimagga and other texts into Chinese at the Liang court in the early 6th century.

name: Anuruddha (ācariya)

scholarly.text: c. 10th–12th c. (contested; estimates range from the 8th to the 12th c.)

summary: Author of the Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha, the Nāmarūpapariccheda and (perhaps) the Paramatthavinicchaya.

name: Sāriputta of Polonnaruwa
summary: Leading scholar-monk of the 12th-century Sri Lankan revival under Parakkamabāhu I, author of the Sāratthadīpanī, the Sāratthamañjūsā and the Vinayasaṅgaha.

name: Sumaṅgala (author of the Vibhāvinī)
summary: Pupil of Sāriputta, author of the Abhidhammatthavibhāvinī-ṭīkā on the Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha.

name: Kassapa (of the Cola country)
summary: Author of the Mohavicchedanī on the Abhidhamma mātikās.

name: Khema (author of the Khemappakaraṇa)
summary: Elder credited with a short Abhidhamma manual.

name: Chapaṭa (Saddhammajotipāla)
summary: Burmese monk who studied in Sri Lanka in the late 12th century and returned to Pagan; credited with the Saṅkhepavaṇṇanā on the Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha.

name: Mahānāma (author of the Mahāvaṃsa)
summary: Elder of the Mahāvihāra tradition credited with composing the Mahāvaṃsa.

name: Mahānāma (author of the Saddhammappakāsinī)
summary: Author of the commentary on the Paṭisambhidāmagga.

name: Upasena (author of the Saddhammapajjotikā)
summary: Author of the commentary on the Niddesa.

name: Moggaliputta Tissa
summary: The elder who, according to the Theravāda chronicles and commentaries, presided over the Third Council at Pāṭaliputta under Asoka, expelled holders of wrong views, composed the Kathāvatthu and sent missions to other lands including Mahinda's to Lanka.

name: Sāriputta
summary: In the Abhidhamma tradition's account, the disciple to whom the Buddha taught the method of the Abhidhamma each day at Lake Anotatta and who taught it to his pupils; the numerical sequence of the Paṭṭhāna is credited to him (Atthasālinī).
notes: U37 contributes only the Abhidhamma-transmission account; U36 owns the full entry.

name: Ledi Sayadaw
summary: Burmese scholar-monk (1846–1923) who wrote more than a hundred works in Pali and Burmese, founded the Ledi forest monastery near Monywa, and taught insight meditation and the Abhidhamma to laypeople — the source of the U Ba Khin – Goenka lineage.
notes: Ordination name given as U Ñāṇa / Ñāṇadhaja (moderate confidence).

name: Saya Thetgyi
summary: Burmese lay meditation teacher (U Po Thet, 1873–1945), a farmer taught by Ledi Sayadaw, who taught insight through awareness of sensation to laypeople and was the teacher of U Ba Khin.

name: Sayagyi U Ba Khin
summary: Burmese government official (Accountant-General) and lay meditation teacher (1899–1971), pupil of Saya Thetgyi, who founded the International Meditation Centre in Rangoon (1952) and taught Goenka.

name: S. N. Goenka
summary: Burma-born Indian businessman turned lay teacher (1924–2013), pupil of U Ba Khin, who taught ten-day Vipassana courses in India from 1969 and founded a worldwide network of centres (Dhamma Giri, Igatpuri, 1976).

name: Webu Sayadaw
summary: Burmese forest monk (1896–1977) renowned for his attainments and for teaching simple, continuous awareness of the breath at the nostrils; admired by U Ba Khin.

name: Mingun Jetavana Sayadaw
summary: Burmese meditation master (U Nārada, 1868–1955) who revived satipaṭṭhāna practice in the early 20th century and taught Mahāsi Sayadaw.

name: Mahāsi Sayadaw
summary: Burmese scholar-meditator (U Sobhana, 1904–1982), pupil of Mingun Jetavana Sayadaw, head of the Sāsana Yeiktha from 1949 and questioner at the Sixth Council (1954–56); his noting method spread across Asia and to the West.

name: Sayadaw U Paṇḍita
summary: Senior Mahāsi-tradition teacher (1921–2016), abbot of Paṇḍitārāma, Yangon, known for rigorous retreats; author of In This Very Life.

name: Nyanaponika Thera
summary: German-born Sri Lankan monk (1901–1994), co-founder of the Buddhist Publication Society, who trained in the Mahāsi method and presented satipaṭṭhāna as 'bare attention' in The Heart of Buddhist Meditation.

name: Ñāṇamoli Thera
summary: English monk in Sri Lanka (1905–1960) whose translation The Path of Purification (1956) made the Visuddhimagga available in English.

name: Anagārika Munindra
summary: Indian Bengali Barua lay teacher (1915–2003) trained with Mahāsi Sayadaw, who taught at Bodh Gaya and influenced the first Western insight teachers.

name: Dipa Ma
summary: Indian laywoman meditation master (Nani Bala Barua, 1911–1989), trained in the Mahāsi method, renowned for her attainments and her teaching of householders.

name: Sunlun Sayadaw

realization_account.text: The tradition holds that he attained arahantship through his own vigorous practice.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Burmese farmer who became a monk (U Kawi, 1878–1952) and, with little scriptural learning, developed a vigorous method of mindfulness of breathing and touch.

name: Pa-Auk Sayadaw
summary: Burmese abbot of Pa-Auk Forest Monastery (Bhaddanta Āciṇṇa, b. 1934), teacher of the full Visuddhimagga system of calm and insight.

name: Mogok Sayadaw
summary: Burmese teacher (U Vimala, 1899–1962) whose insight method begins from understanding dependent origination.

name: Kheminda Thera
summary: Sri Lankan monk, co-translator of the Vimuttimagga (The Path of Freedom, 1961) and a critic of the Burmese satipaṭṭhāna method's claims for insight without jhāna.
notes: Role in the Mahāsi controversy recalled with low confidence.

name: Ajahn Sao Kantasīlo
summary: Thai Dhammayut monk (1861–1941), austere meditation master and teacher of Ajahn Mun; with him the founder of the forest tradition.

name: Ajahn Mun Bhūridatto

realization_account.text: His disciples' biographies say he attained arahantship in a cave in Chiang Mai province, after years of solitary practice and visions.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Thai forest master (1870–1949) who revived the dhutaṅga wandering life in the forests of Isan and northern Thailand; teacher of nearly all later forest masters.

name: Ajahn Lee Dhammadharo
summary: Thai forest master (1907–1961), pupil of Ajahn Mun, known for his systematic breath meditation (Keeping the Breath in Mind) and founder of Wat Asokaram.

name: Ajahn Maha Boowa Ñāṇasampanno
summary: Thai forest master (1913–2011) of Wat Pa Baan Taad, pupil and biographer of Ajahn Mun, who taught an energetic path of body contemplation and wisdom culminating in seeing through the radiant citta.

name: Ajahn Chah Subhaddo
summary: Thai forest master (1918–1992) of Wat Nong Pah Pong in Ubon Ratchathani, who met Ajahn Mun briefly and founded a large lineage of monasteries including Wat Pah Nanachat for Western monks.

name: Ajahn Thate Desaransi
summary: Thai forest master (1902–1994), pupil of Ajahn Mun, abbot of Wat Hin Mark Peng.

name: Ajahn Fuang Jotiko
summary: Thai forest monk (1915–1986), pupil of Ajahn Lee and teacher of Ṭhānissaro Bhikkhu.

name: Luang Pu Dune Atulo
summary: Thai forest master of Surin (1888–1983), pupil of Ajahn Mun, known for his teaching that the mind that sends itself out is the origin of suffering and the mind seeing the mind is the path.

name: Mae Chee Kaew Sianglam

realization_account.text: Her biography (by Ajahn Dick Sīlaratano) presents her as having attained arahantship.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Thai forest nun (1901–1991), pupil of Ajahn Mun and Ajahn Maha Boowa, whose biography records her visionary meditation and her attainment.

name: Ajahn Sumedho
summary: American-born senior Western disciple of Ajahn Chah (b. 1934), founder of Chithurst and Amaravati monasteries in England.

name: Ṭhānissaro Bhikkhu
summary: American forest monk (Geoffrey DeGraff, b. 1949), pupil of Ajahn Fuang, abbot of Metta Forest Monastery and translator of Ajahn Lee, Ajahn Mun and much of the Pali canon.

name: Buddhadāsa Bhikkhu
summary: Thai reformist monk (1906–1993), founder of Suan Mokkh (1932), who taught voidness of self, present-moment dependent origination and mindfulness with breathing, and engaged in dialogue with other religions.

name: P. A. Payutto
summary: Thai scholar-monk (b. 1938), author of Buddhadhamma, a systematic exposition of the canon, and of a critique of the Dhammakāya teaching that nibbāna is a self.

name: Luang Pu Sodh Candasaro

realization_account.text: The tradition holds that in 1917 he penetrated to the Dhammakāya after resolving not to rise until he had seen the Dhamma the Buddha saw.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Thai abbot of Wat Paknam Bhasicharoen (1884–1959), founder of the Dhammakāya meditation method (vijjā dhammakāya).

name: Luang Por Dhammajayo
summary: Thai monk (b. 1944), co-founder (1970) and long-time abbot of Wat Phra Dhammakaya.

name: Vajirañāṇa (King Mongkut)
summary: Siamese prince who spent 27 years as a monk (1824–1851), founded the reformist Dhammayut order, and reigned as King Rāma IV (1851–1868).

name: Välivita Saraṇaṅkara
summary: Sri Lankan monk (1698–1778) who led the 18th-century revival and, after higher ordination was restored by Siamese monks in 1753, became the first Saṅgharāja of the Siyam Nikāya.

name: Upāli Thera (of Ayutthaya)
summary: Siamese elder who led the mission of 1753 that restored higher ordination in Kandy; the borān meditation manuals of Sri Lanka are associated with this mission.
